subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What is red-shift?
options: Light from distant galaxies shifted towards longer (redder) wavelengths
Light being absorbed by red dust
questions.explain: Red-shift is the increase in observed wavelength of light from galaxies moving away from us.

questions.q: The expansion of the universe from a single point is described by which theory?
questions.explain: The Big Bang theory says the universe began from a very small, hot, dense point and has been expanding.

questions.q: Which of these correctly describes our solar system?
options: One star, eight planets, plus dwarf planets and moons
Only the Sun and the Earth
questions.explain: Our solar system contains one star (the Sun), eight planets, several dwarf planets (such as Pluto) and many moons (natural satellites).

questions.q: The cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation is considered:
options: Evidence for the Big Bang theory
Proof that the universe is shrinking
questions.explain: The CMB is faint microwave radiation from across the sky, regarded as strong evidence for the Big Bang.

questions.q: What is at the centre of our solar system?
options: The Sun, which is a star
questions.explain: The Sun, a star, is at the centre of the solar system. The eight planets, dwarf planets and their moons orbit it.

questions.q: More distant galaxies generally show a:
options: Greater red-shift, meaning they move away faster
questions.explain: More distant galaxies have greater red-shifts, indicating they are receding faster.

questions.q: A low polar orbit satellite is useful for:
options: Live television broadcasting to one fixed dish
Scanning the whole surface of the Earth, e.g. for weather and imaging
questions.explain: Low polar orbiting satellites pass over different parts of the Earth as it rotates, ideal for imaging and weather monitoring.

questions.q: A geostationary satellite:
options: Stays above the same point on the Earth's equator
Orbits over the poles many times a day
Does not move at all in space
questions.explain: A geostationary satellite orbits once every 24 hours above the equator, staying over the same point.

questions.q: If a satellite moves to a higher orbit (larger radius), to stay in a stable orbit it must travel:
questions.explain: At a larger orbital radius the gravitational force is weaker, so a slower orbital speed is needed for a stable orbit.

questions.q: For an object in a stable circular orbit, the centripetal force is directed:
questions.explain: The centripetal force always acts towards the centre of the orbit.

questions.q: How does the red-shift of a galaxy relate to its distance from Earth?
options: Red-shift is the same for all galaxies
More distant galaxies have a smaller red-shift
More distant galaxies have a larger red-shift, showing they recede faster
questions.explain: The more distant a galaxy, the greater its red-shift, meaning it is moving away faster. This is evidence that the whole universe is expanding.

questions.q: During its main sequence, a star is stable because:
options: There are no forces acting on it
The inward gravitational force is balanced by the outward force from fusion
questions.explain: In the main sequence, gravity pulling inward is balanced by the outward pressure from nuclear fusion.

questions.q: A natural satellite of a planet is best described as:
questions.explain: A moon is a natural satellite that orbits a planet.

questions.q: A star about the same size as the Sun will eventually become a:
options: Red giant then a white dwarf
questions.explain: A Sun-sized star expands into a red giant and then collapses to form a white dwarf.

questions.q: A massive star much bigger than the Sun can end its life as a:
options: Neutron star or black hole after a supernova
Nebula that never forms a star
questions.explain: A massive star explodes as a supernova, leaving behind a neutron star or, if massive enough, a black hole.

questions.q: To find the time t in the equation P = E / t, which rearrangement is correct?
questions.explain: Starting from P = E/t, multiply both sides by t then divide by P: t = E / P. A common error is to write t = P/E by inverting the wrong way.

questions.q: The observation that light from distant galaxies is red-shifted tells us that:
options: The galaxies are moving away from us
The galaxies are moving towards us
questions.explain: Red-shift shows distant galaxies are moving away, which is evidence the universe is expanding.

questions.q: What is the first stage in the formation of a star?
options: A cloud of gas and dust called a nebula
questions.explain: Stars form from a nebula, a cloud of gas and dust pulled together by gravity.

questions.q: Comets are objects that:
options: Are made of solid iron only
Orbit the Sun in highly elliptical orbits and often have tails
questions.explain: Comets follow very elongated elliptical orbits around the Sun and form tails as they approach it.

questions.q: What provides the centripetal force that keeps a planet in orbit around the Sun?
questions.explain: Gravitational attraction between the Sun and planet provides the centripetal force for the orbit.

questions.q: Which object is at the centre of our solar system?
questions.explain: The Sun, a star, lies at the centre of the solar system.

questions.q: For a stable orbit at a fixed radius, an object must travel at:
questions.explain: A stable orbit at a given radius requires a specific orbital speed.
